subject: Biology
category: Cell Division, Principles of Genetics, Variations and Heredity
question:
a) Explain the following terms:
(i) Recessive gene (2½ marks)
(ii) Homeostatic imbalance. (2½ marks)
(iii) Nitrogenous waste products (2½ marks)
(iv) Inbreeding (2½ marks)
modelAnswer:
Note: the left edge of the photo cuts off the question number and the part letters for (b) and (c); they are inferred from the order of the parts.

(i) A recessive gene (allele) is one whose effect is masked in the presence of a dominant allele, so it is expressed in the phenotype only when it is present in two copies (homozygous recessive, e.g. aa). Examples: the alleles for albinism and sickle-cell anaemia.

(ii) Homeostatic imbalance is the failure of the body's homeostatic mechanisms to keep the internal environment (e.g. body temperature, blood glucose, water and salt balance, blood pH) within its normal narrow range. It can result from disease, ageing, injury or extreme conditions, and leads to disorders such as diabetes mellitus (failure of blood sugar control), dehydration, hypothermia or hyperthermia, and high blood pressure.

(iii) Nitrogenous waste products are the nitrogen-containing waste substances formed from the breakdown (deamination) of excess amino acids and nucleic acids. The main ones are ammonia (very toxic, excreted by most aquatic animals such as fish and Amoeba), urea (less toxic, excreted by mammals and amphibians) and uric acid (least toxic and insoluble, excreted by birds, reptiles and insects). Others include creatinine and guanine.

(iv) Inbreeding is the mating (breeding) of closely related individuals (e.g. brother and sister, parent and offspring), or self-pollination in plants. It increases homozygosity, helping to fix desirable traits and produce pure lines, but it also increases the chance of harmful recessive alleles being expressed, leading to reduced vigour and fertility (inbreeding depression).

subject: Biology
category: Cell Division, Principles of Genetics, Variations and Heredity
question:
Assuming a hairless cat has a genotype of (Hh) and inheriting a dominant allele (H) makes the cat hairless. Inheriting two of the dominant allele is lethal.
(i). Use the Punnet Square to show the offspring's of a cross between a male and a female hairless cat.
(ii). Show the genotypes and phenotypes from the cross.
(iii). What is the genotypic ratio of the cross?
(iv). Show the phenotypic ratio of the cross
(v). Calculate the percentages for mortality, hairless and hairy offspring from the cross. (20 marks)
modelAnswer:
(i) Parents: Hh (hairless male) × Hh (hairless female).
Gametes: H and h from each parent.
Punnett square:
| | H | h |
| H | HH | Hh |
| h | Hh | hh |

(ii)
HH: dies (lethal).
Hh (2 squares): hairless.
hh: hairy (normal coat).

(iii) Genotypic ratio: 1 HH : 2 Hh : 1 hh.

(iv) Phenotypic ratio at conception: 1 dead : 2 hairless : 1 hairy. Among the surviving offspring: 2 hairless : 1 hairy.

(v) Out of 4 offspring conceived:
Mortality (HH): 1/4 × 100 = 25%.
Hairless (Hh): 2/4 × 100 = 50%.
Hairy (hh): 1/4 × 100 = 25%.
(Among the live kittens only: hairless 2/3 = 66.7%, hairy 1/3 = 33.3%.)

subject: Biology
question:
(a). Draw and label the diagram of a mammalian brain, giving one function of any five (5) labeled parts. (15 marks)
(b). Outline ten (10) functions of the mammalian liver. (5 marks)
modelAnswer:
(a) Diagram: a vertical (longitudinal) section of the mammalian brain showing the large cerebrum (two cerebral hemispheres with a folded cortex) at the front and top; the corpus callosum joining the hemispheres; the thalamus and hypothalamus below the cerebrum, with the pituitary gland attached under the hypothalamus; the pineal body; the midbrain (with optic lobes/corpora quadrigemina); the cerebellum at the back below the cerebrum; the pons and medulla oblongata leading into the spinal cord; the meninges and ventricles may also be shown.
Functions (any five):
Cerebrum: controls voluntary actions, intelligence, memory, reasoning, speech and learning, and interprets sensations (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell).
Cerebellum: coordinates muscular movements and maintains balance and posture.
Medulla oblongata: controls involuntary actions such as breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and sneezing.
Hypothalamus: regulates body temperature, thirst, hunger, water balance and sleep, and controls the pituitary gland.
Pituitary gland: secretes hormones that control other endocrine glands and growth.
Thalamus: relays sensory impulses to the cerebral cortex.
Pons: relays impulses between the cerebrum and cerebellum; helps control breathing.
Corpus callosum: connects and coordinates the two cerebral hemispheres.
Midbrain/optic lobes: visual and auditory reflexes.

(b) Any ten:
1. Regulation of blood sugar (stores glucose as glycogen; releases glucose).
2. Deamination of excess amino acids and formation of urea (ornithine cycle).
3. Production of bile (for emulsifying fats).
4. Storage of vitamins (A, D, B12) and minerals (iron, copper).
5. Detoxification of poisons, drugs and alcohol.
6. Production of heat (thermoregulation).
7. Synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin).
8. Breakdown of old red blood cells and haemoglobin (bile pigments).
9. Formation of red blood cells in the foetus.
10. Fat metabolism: synthesis of cholesterol and lipoproteins; conversion of carbohydrates to fat.
11. Transamination (making non-essential amino acids).
12. Storage of blood.
13. Inactivation of hormones.

subject: Biology
category: Cell Division, Principles of Genetics, Variations and Heredity
question:
Explain the following:
(a) Cytokinesis in cell division (10 marks)
(b) Diploblastic organization in Hydra (5 marks)
(c) Reproduction in reptiles (5 marks)
modelAnswer:
(a) Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm of a cell to form two daughter cells, usually at the end of nuclear division (mitosis or meiosis), during late anaphase and telophase.
In animal cells: a ring of actin and myosin filaments (the contractile ring) forms beneath the cell membrane at the equator. It contracts, forming a cleavage furrow that deepens until the cell is pinched into two.
In plant cells: because of the rigid cell wall, no furrow forms. Instead, vesicles from the Golgi apparatus, carrying cell-wall material, gather at the equator (guided by the phragmoplast) and fuse to form a cell plate. The cell plate grows outwards until it joins the parent cell wall, and a new cell wall (middle lamella of pectin, then cellulose) is laid down between the two daughter cells.
Cytokinesis shares the organelles and cytoplasm between the daughter cells. If it does not occur, a multinucleate cell (coenocyte) results.

(b) Hydra is diploblastic: its body wall is made of only two layers of cells, the outer ectoderm (epidermis) and the inner endoderm (gastrodermis), separated by a non-cellular, jelly-like mesogloea. The ectoderm contains musculo-epithelial cells, interstitial cells, nerve cells and cnidoblasts (stinging cells) for protection and capturing prey; the endoderm contains nutritive-muscular cells and gland cells for digestion. It encloses a single gut cavity (enteron) with one opening (the mouth). There is no true mesoderm and no body cavity (coelom).

(c) Reproduction in reptiles:
Sexes are separate; fertilisation is internal (males transfer sperm by hemipenes, or a penis in turtles and crocodiles), which is an adaptation to life on land.
Most reptiles are oviparous, laying shelled (amniotic) eggs on land, often buried in sand or soil and warmed by the sun; the leathery or calcareous shell and the embryonic membranes (amnion, chorion, allantois, yolk sac) protect the embryo from drying and supply food (yolk). Some snakes and lizards are ovoviviparous or viviparous.
There is no larval stage: the young hatch as miniature adults (direct development). Parental care is usually little, though crocodiles guard their nests and young. In some species (e.g. crocodiles, turtles), the incubation temperature determines the sex of the young.

subject: Biology
category: Living Things in Nature and Biological Molecules
question: Briefly explain the four (4) main types of organic molecules in a cell (20 marks)
modelAnswer:
1. Carbohydrates: compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen with the general formula Cx(H₂O)y. Types: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose, formed by glycosidic bonds) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin). Functions: main source of energy (glucose in respiration), energy storage (starch in plants, glycogen in animals), structural (cellulose cell walls, chitin), part of nucleotides (ribose, deoxyribose).

2. Lipids (fats and oils): compounds of C, H and O with relatively little oxygen, insoluble in water. Triglycerides are formed from one glycerol and three fatty acids (ester bonds); fatty acids may be saturated (fats, solid) or unsaturated (oils, liquid). Phospholipids form cell membranes; steroids include cholesterol and hormones. Functions: energy store (give about twice the energy of carbohydrates), insulation, protection of organs, waterproofing, membranes, hormones.

3. Proteins: compounds of C, H, O and N (often S), made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. There are about 20 amino acids. Structure: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix, β-sheet), tertiary (3-D folding) and quaternary (several chains). Functions: enzymes (catalysts), structural (keratin, collagen), transport (haemoglobin), hormones (insulin), antibodies, contraction (actin, myosin), and energy source.

4. Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA): polymers of nucleotides, each made of a pentose sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine in DNA, or uracil in RNA). DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–T, G–C); it stores genetic information. RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is single-stranded and takes part in protein synthesis. Related molecules: ATP (energy carrier).

subject: Biology
question: With the aid of well labeled diagram, explain the mechanism of perception of taste in man. (20 marks)
modelAnswer:
Diagram: (1) the tongue in surface view, showing papillae (circumvallate papillae at the back in a V shape, fungiform papillae at the tip and sides, foliate papillae at the sides) and the traditional areas of taste; (2) a taste bud in section, showing the taste pore, taste hairs (microvilli), gustatory (receptor) cells, supporting cells, basal cells and sensory nerve fibres leaving at the base, embedded in the epithelium of the tongue.

Mechanism:
1. Taste (gustation) is a chemical sense. The receptors are taste buds, found mainly on the papillae of the tongue, and also on the soft palate, pharynx and epiglottis.
2. Food chemicals must dissolve in saliva before they can be tasted. The dissolved substances enter the taste pore and come into contact with the taste hairs (microvilli) of the gustatory cells.
3. The chemicals bind to specific receptor proteins (for sweet, bitter and umami) or pass through ion channels (salty: Na⁺; sour: H⁺) in the membrane of the receptor cells. This causes depolarisation (a receptor potential).
4. The receptor cells release neurotransmitters onto the sensory neurones, generating nerve impulses.
5. Impulses travel along the facial nerve (VII, front two-thirds of the tongue), the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX, back one-third) and the vagus nerve (X, pharynx and epiglottis) to the medulla oblongata, then the thalamus, and finally to the gustatory area of the cerebral cortex (parietal lobe), where the taste is interpreted.
6. The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Flavour depends also on smell: when the nose is blocked (e.g. a cold), food seems tasteless. Taste helps in selecting food, rejecting harmful substances (bitter, sour) and stimulating secretion of saliva and gastric juice.

subject: Biology
category: Ecologic and Economic Importance of Animals
question:
(a). Copy and complete (*) the table below: (5 marks)
(b). Explain the process of excretion in protozoa (5 marks)
(c). Outline five (5) disadvantages of asexual reproduction. (5 marks)
(d). Briefly explain divergent evolution. (5 marks)
modelAnswer:
(a) Completed table:
1. Vector: mosquito (Culex for lymphatic filariasis; Anopheles for malaria) | Lymphatic filariasis, Malaria | Parasite.
2. Lice | Typhus, louse-borne relapsing fever | Pathogen: bacteria (Rickettsia prowazekii causes typhus; Borrelia recurrentis causes relapsing fever).
3. Vector: sandfly (Phlebotomus/Lutzomyia) | Leishmaniasis | Parasite.
4. Ticks | Disease: Lyme disease (also tick-borne relapsing fever, Rocky Mountain spotted fever) | Bacteria.
5. Tsetse flies | Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) | Pathogen: parasite (the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei).

(b) In protozoa (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium), excretion of nitrogenous waste (mainly ammonia) and carbon dioxide takes place by simple diffusion across the cell membrane into the surrounding water, helped by the large surface area-to-volume ratio of the small body. Freshwater protozoa also have contractile vacuoles, which collect excess water (entering by osmosis), together with some dissolved wastes, and discharge it to the outside periodically; this is mainly osmoregulation. Paramecium has two contractile vacuoles with radiating canals.

(c) Any five:
1. No genetic variation: offspring are identical to the parent, so populations cannot adapt easily to changes in the environment.
2. Harmful characteristics or mutations are passed on to all offspring.
3. A disease or pest can wipe out the whole population, since all individuals are equally susceptible.
4. Overcrowding near the parent leads to competition for space, light, water and nutrients.
5. It does not contribute to evolution through new combinations of genes.
6. Some methods (e.g. vegetative propagation) give limited means of dispersal.
7. Vigour may decline over many generations (accumulation of diseases, e.g. viruses in vegetatively propagated crops).

(d) Divergent evolution is the process by which a group of related organisms descended from a common ancestor become increasingly different from one another over time, as they adapt to different environments or ways of life (different selection pressures). It leads to homologous structures, which have the same basic structure and origin but different functions, e.g. the pentadactyl limb modified as the arm of man, the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the foreleg of a horse. When divergence produces many species from one ancestor, it is called adaptive radiation (e.g. Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands with beaks adapted to different foods).
